narrative.text: The morning edition of the Ashenmere Chronicle lands on your desk at 06:48 with a front-page headline that takes approximately one second to end your political career, or would, if the career-ending were the only thing at stake. The headline reads: SECRET MOBILIZATION — ARMY MOVES BY NIGHT AS CHANCELLOR DENIES CRISIS. Below the headline are photographs. Grainy, clearly taken from a distance, unmistakably showing military convoys on the northern roads under blackout conditions. The byline is Nadia Voss. Of course it is Nadia Voss. It is always Nadia Voss when something that was supposed to be secret becomes public, and the particular injustice of the situation is that Voss is doing exactly what a free press is supposed to do and you cannot even be angry at her without being angry at the principle of press freedom that you have spent your chancellorship defending.

Three sources confirmed. The photographs came from a railway worker who noticed military rolling stock moving through the Kravenstal yards at 02:00. He called a cousin who works for the Chronicle. The cousin called Voss. Voss called the Ministry of Defense for comment — standard procedure, which means someone at the Ministry confirmed the mobilization rather than issuing a denial. Either we have a leak in the Ministry or we have a patriot in the Ministry who believes the public has a right to know they are about to be at war. The distinction is academic. The result is the same. The Parliament has already issued a statement demanding you address the chamber by noon. The Tyvaren embassy has issued a statement calling the mobilization a 'provocation inconsistent with diplomatic dialogue.' The international press is running the photographs. We have approximately four hours before the narrative is permanently outside our control.

The secret mobilization was always going to be discovered. I knew that when I ordered it. Brenner knew it. Vyktor knew it. The question was never whether it would be discovered — it was whether the discovery would happen before or after the mobilization was complete enough to matter. It has happened before. The mobilization is partial. The convoys Voss photographed represent perhaps forty percent of the planned movements. The remaining sixty percent is still possible if I move fast enough. But moving fast means giving orders while the political firestorm is burning, and the firestorm is already visible from the window — there are journalists gathering at the palace gate, and somewhere in the Parliament building Drazen Kolvar is drafting a speech about executive overreach and the death of democratic accountability, and the speech will be very good because Kolvar's speeches are always very good when he is defending the principle that Chancellors should not do things without asking his permission.

Military status. The mobilization is at approximately forty percent of planned capacity. The remaining movements can be accelerated if we drop the concealment protocols — open movement during daylight hours triples our throughput. Alternatively, we can freeze the mobilization in place and maintain the forty percent we have already deployed. Either decision has military consequences. Freezing means we face Vukov with partial readiness. Accelerating means we face the political crisis with full transparency. I cannot advise you on the political dimension. I can tell you that from a purely military perspective, partial mobilization is worse than either full mobilization or no mobilization. It gives us the political cost of preparation without the military benefit of completion.

Dusek delivers this assessment with the same calm she uses to report supply figures. She is not judging the political situation because judging the political situation is not her job. Her job is to tell you what the military needs and then execute whatever decision you make. The fact that she is standing in your office at dawn while journalists mass at the gate and your government trembles on the edge of a confidence crisis is, to her, simply the environment in which the decision must be made. You envy her clarity. You do not have the luxury of clarity. You have the luxury of being Chancellor, which means you have to hold the military reality and the political reality and the personal reality in your head simultaneously and make a decision that addresses all three while satisfying none.

choices.text: "Schedule a press conference for nine o'clock. I will tell the country exactly what I ordered, when I ordered it, and why. The secret mobilization was not a conspiracy — it was a defensive measure taken during a period of diplomatic sensitivity. I wanted to prepare without provoking. I was wrong about the provocation, or perhaps I was right about the preparation and wrong about the secrecy. Either way, the country deserves to hear the truth from me, not from a leaked photograph. And Vyktor — I want the full mobilization order issued simultaneously with my statement. If the secret is out, let the preparation be complete."

"Deny the story. Issue a statement that the photographs show routine logistical movements — exercises, not mobilization. Have the Ministry of Defense produce documentation confirming previously scheduled training operations in the northern sector. And Vyktor — I want a quiet conversation with the Chronicle's publisher. Not a threat. A reminder that publishing unverified photographs during a national security crisis is not journalism. It is aiding the enemy. Nadia Voss is a patriot. Make her understand that this time, her patriotism and her profession are in conflict."

"Change the story. The secret mobilization was a phased approach, and the first phase was quiet out of operational necessity. Phase Two begins now, in public, with full transparency. I'll address the nation at noon from the Ministry of Defense, with General Brenner at my side, and I will frame this not as a secret that was exposed but as a plan that is advancing to its next stage. The photographs are not a leak. They are documentation of Phase One. The press conference is Phase Two. We are not scrambling to explain a scandal. We are executing a communication strategy that was always designed to transition from covert to overt at the appropriate moment. The appropriate moment is now."
